supporting literacy development. Some narrative reviews of quasi-experimental studies report that ICT is indeed effective in naturalistic
teacher-delivered ﬁeld-based intervention trials (Bolstad, 2004; Macarthur, Ferretti, Okolo, & Cavalier, 2001), whereas other narrative
reviews are rather cautious in interpreting ﬁndings and argue that the results may be due to inadequate research designs in many of the
studies included in the reviews (e.g. Blok, Oostdam, Otter, & Overmaat, 2002). To this latter end, the strongest evidence of intervention
effectiveness for ICT comes from three comprehensive systematic reviews (see Ehri et al., 2001; Slavin, Cheung, Groff, & Lake, 2008;
Torgerson & Zhu, 2004) and a ‘tertiary’ review in which many systematic reviews are included for a further review (Torgerson, 2007).

3.2.4. Test-phase attractiveness ratings
An analysis of the test-phase attractiveness ratings
(Table 3) showed a significant main effect of behavioral
history [F(2,83)=3.89, p=.02, η2=.09]. Cheater faces were
less attractive than other faces [F(1,84)=5.65, p=.02,
η2=.06], whereas attractiveness did not differ between
faces associated with irrelevant and trustworthy behavior
[F(1,84)=1.74, p=.19, η2=.02]. Faces associated with
exceptional and ordinary behavior were equally attractive
[F(1,84)=0.07, p =.80, η2b.01]. There was no interaction
between the two variables [F(2,83)=2.97, p=.06, η2=.07].
